snippet.title: Where did Princess Diana's clothes go #royal #princess #queenelizabeth #history
snippet.description:
What happened to Princess Diana's clothes after her death? 
You might think Kate and Meghan inherited her iconic wardrobe—but they didn't.
Before Diana's belongings were sorted, her butler destroyed some of her most personal items, including lingerie, swimsuits, and sportswear, to protect her privacy and keep them out of collectors' hands.
But most of Diana's famous wardrobe had already found a new purpose.
Every winter, she donated coats to people in need.
And just two months before her death, Diana auctioned off more than 70 of her dresses, raising over $3 million for charity.
Some of her most iconic gowns were preserved by the royal family and can still be seen in royal exhibitions today.
Even after her death, Princess Diana's wardrobe continued changing lives.

snippet.title: The Woman Who Would Be King: Egypt’s Stolen History.
snippet.description:
"The Woman Who Would Be King: Egypt’s Stolen History."

History remembers Cleopatra. But she wasn't the first woman to rule Egypt as a king—and she wasn't even the most powerful.
For three millennia, ancient Egyptian kingship was defined by a rigid patriarchal model. The Pharaoh was the "Living Horus," a male solar deity responsible for maintaining Ma’at—the cosmic balance of truth and justice. Yet, when the traditional mechanisms of power failed, a handful of extraordinary women did the unthinkable: they didn't just rule as queens; they ascended the throne as sovereign Pharaohs.
In this documentary, we uncover the lives of the "Sovereign Shadows"—powerful women like Sobekneferu, Hatshepsut, Nefertiti, and Twosret—and investigate the systematic campaign known as damnatio memoriae that attempted to strike their names from eternity.

In this video, you will discover:
The Crocodile Queen: How Sobekneferu (c. 1806 BCE) became the first confirmed female King, blending masculine and feminine iconography to stabilize a dying dynasty.

The Woman Who Was King: The meteoric rise of Hatshepsut, whose 22-year reign marked a golden age of trade and monumental building, only for her successors to chisel her face from history.

The Ghost Pharaoh: The stunning evidence that Nefertiti may have ruled as the shadowy Pharaoh Neferneferuaten, with her royal treasures later repurposed to bury the boy-king, Tutankhamun.

Ruler of Chaos: The embattled reign of Twosret, whose magnificent tomb in the Valley of the Kings (KV14) was stolen and plastered over by her male successor.

The Final Link: How Cleopatra VII used the legacy of these women to challenge Rome, only to have her own story rewritten by the propaganda of the winners.

Why were they erased? In ancient Egypt, your name (Ren) was a vital part of your soul. To erase a name from a monument was an eternal punishment, intended to ensure the individual did not exist in the afterlife. These women were seen as a "structural anomaly" that needed to be corrected to restore the traditional male line.
But you cannot kill the truth. snippet.title: What happened to Queen’s wardrobe after her death #royal #queenelizabeth
snippet.description:
What really happened to Queen Elizabeth’s massive wardrobe after her death?
And why are some of her outfits now considered national treasures?

After Queen Elizabeth passed away, one surprising detail shocked many people:
she almost never wore the same outfit twice.

Every look she wore became part of British history.
That’s why her most iconic outfits are now being preserved in museums.

Among them are her wedding dress, her coronation gown and robe,
and the outfit she wore when Charles was officially named Prince of Wales.

These pieces will now be protected as part of Britain’s royal heritage
and displayed for the public.

But her jewelry collection stayed within the royal family.
Queen Camilla and Princess Kate are now expected to wear
Elizabeth’s tiaras, necklaces, earrings, and brooches.

Imagine wearing jewelry that witnessed an entire era of history.

snippet.title: Prince Harry to visit UK with family
snippet.description:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are bringing their two children to Britain for the first time in more than four years. 

Prince Archie, now aged seven, and Princess Lilibet, aged five, last visited the UK in 2022 during the late Queen Elizabeth II’s platinum jubilee celebrations. 

Last year, Prince Harry lost his battle against the Home Office for automatic police protection while in Britain. He previously claimed it was not safe to bring his family without it. 

Harry plans to bring his family to an event next month, promoting the one year countdown to his Invictus Games for wounded veterans. The Invictus Games will be held in Birmingham in 2027. 

His Majesty King Charles hasn’t seen Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet since 2022.  

Last September, Prince Harry met with his father, the King at Clarence House in London, their first face-to-face meeting since 2024.  

This meeting was seen by many as a first step towards improving relations between them. 

According to The Guardian, a source reportedly said; “Harry says he’s coming back before the end of the year with the children with the express intent to reunite with his dad.”

snippet.title: Princess William doesn’t wear wedding ring #royal #princewilliam #princesscatherine
snippet.description:
Have you ever noticed that Prince William never wears a wedding ring? 
Many people assume it means something is wrong in his marriage to Kate. But that's not the case.
The real reason is much simpler: William has never liked wearing jewelry. Before the wedding, Kensington Palace even confirmed that he had chosen not to wear a wedding band.
Interestingly, he's not the only royal. Prince Philip never wore one either, while King Charles wore his wedding ring tucked beneath his signet ring.
Prince Harry is the exception—he's almost always seen wearing his wedding band.
So for Prince William, skipping the ring isn't a sign of trouble—it's simply personal preference and a long-standing royal tradition.

snippet.title: The Man Behind The Scenes of The British Monarchy. #history #royalhistory
snippet.description:
Alexander Cambridge was born on April 14 1874 and at birth received the grand title of Prince of Teck. His lineage staggered the imagination. He was a great grandson of King George III and the youngest brother of the famous Queen Mary. Later this handsome aristocrat would become the maternal uncle to 2 British monarchs Edward VIII and George VI. His life became a perfect example of how a modest German prince transformed into one of the main pillars of the vast British Empire.
His destiny became closely intertwined with the history of the crown when he married Princess Alice of Albany who was a direct granddaughter of Queen Victoria. During the First World War anti German sentiments forced the British court to change their names. snippet.title: The Royal "Survivor" You've Never Heard Of  #history
snippet.description:
Imagine a wedding gift that survived 2 world wars and the fall of 3 monarchies. In 1913 the German Emperor Wilhelm II commissioned a unique piece of jewelry for his only daughter Princess Victoria Louise. The craftsmen created an incredible diadem of platinum and diamonds in the fashionable neoclassical style. Its main decoration was an ancient Greek meander pattern and 1 large diamond in the very center that swung slightly when walking and dazzlingly caught the light.
This jewel began its long journey through the royal courts of Europe. Victoria Louise gave it to her daughter Frederica when she married the future King Paul I of Greece. The diadem became a true talisman for brides. In 1962 Frederica passed this shining crown to her own daughter Sofia on the day of her wedding to the future Spanish monarch Juan Carlos I. Thus the German tiara found its final home in sunny Spain.
A new wave of worldwide fame came to this piece of jewelry in 2004. It was this elegant diadem that the journalist Letizia Ortiz chose for her wedding to the heir to the throne and now King Felipe VI. Today the Prussian Diamond Tiara remains 1 of the most beloved and frequently worn pieces of the Spanish court. It proves that true masterpieces of jewelry art can unite generations and survive any historical catastrophes.
